# Angiotensin Receptor–Neprilysin Inhibition in Heart Failure: A Narrative Review

## Introduction and rationale

Heart failure (HF) is a complex syndrome driven in part by neurohormonal dysregulation, classically targeted through the renin–angiotensin–aldosterone system (RAAS), the sympathetic nervous system, and the natriuretic peptide system [1]. Neprilysin is a membrane-bound endopeptidase that degrades several biologically active peptides. Neprilysin (also known as neutral endopeptidase or enkephalinase) participates in the degradation of natriuretic and other vasoactive peptides, including bradykinin and adrenomedullin [2]. Neprilysin is an endopeptidase that cleaves a variety of peptides such as natriuretic peptides, bradykinin, adrenomedullin, substance P, angiotensin I and II, and endothelin, and it has a broad role in cardiovascular, renal, pulmonary, gastrointestinal, endocrine, and neurologic functions [3]. Because neprilysin degrades both vasodilatory and vasoconstrictor peptides, its inhibition alone produces mixed effects; the combined angiotensin receptor and neprilysin inhibitor (ARNi) was developed with an intent to increase vasodilatory natriuretic peptides and prevent counterregulatory activation of the angiotensin system [3]. This dual rationale is reviewed in detail elsewhere, including the substrate promiscuity that underlies both potential benefits and risks of the class [4].

Sacubitril/valsartan (LCZ696) is the first-in-class ARNI. Upon oral administration, it delivers systemic exposure of sacubitril, a neprilysin inhibitor prodrug metabolized by esterases to the active metabolite sacubitrilat (LBQ657), and valsartan, an angiotensin receptor blocker; sacubitrilat inhibits degradation of natriuretic peptides and thereby enhances their biological activity [5].

## Pivotal evidence in HFrEF: PARADIGM-HF

The landmark PARADIGM-HF trial established the class. McMurray and colleagues compared angiotensin–neprilysin inhibition with enalapril in heart failure, reporting in the New England Journal of Medicine in 2014 [6]. The efficacy and safety of LCZ696 titrated to a target dose of 200 mg twice daily was evaluated in 8442 patients with HFrEF (LVEF ≤40%), and LCZ696 significantly reduced the primary composite endpoint of cardiovascular death or HF hospitalization by 20% compared with enalapril [5]. Eligible patients were ambulatory, and had received an ACE inhibitor or ARB at doses equivalent to enalapril 10 mg daily for at least 4 weeks, with sequential run-in periods during which all patients received high-dose enalapril and then sacubitril–valsartan before randomization [7]. A prespecified analysis examined the early mortality benefit and optimal dosing of ARNI therapy [8], and benefit was preserved even among patients requiring dose reduction: participants taking lower-than-target sacubitril/valsartan doses had a lower risk of the primary event compared with those taking lower-than-target doses of enalapril [9]. Beyond hard endpoints, patients randomized to sacubitril/valsartan had a smaller decline in KCCQ scores in the setting of a heart failure hospitalization, demonstrating better health-related quality of life in surviving patients [10].

## Mechanisms: reverse remodeling and biomarkers

Mechanistic studies have probed how ARNI improves outcomes. In the open-label PROVE-HF study, reduction in NT-proBNP concentration was weakly yet significantly correlated with improvements in markers of cardiac volume and function at 12 months [11]. In contrast, the randomized EVALUATE-HF trial found that although sacubitril-valsartan reduces cardiovascular mortality and HF hospitalization in HFrEF and these benefits may relate to effects on hemodynamics and cardiac remodeling, the drug did not significantly reduce central aortic stiffness compared with enalapril [12], though favorable effects on cardiac structure were observed [13].

## In-hospital and post-stabilization initiation

PIONEER-HF extended the evidence to hospitalized patients. Whether initiation of sacubitril–valsartan is safe and effective among patients hospitalized for acute decompensated heart failure was unknown; the trial enrolled patients with HFrEF hospitalized for acute decompensation [14], and demonstrated a greater reduction in NT-proBNP versus enalapril [15]. The TRANSITION study complemented this by comparing pre- versus post-discharge initiation; sacubitril/valsartan is indicated for chronic HFrEF, and TRANSITION provided evidence of safety and tolerability when initiated early after decompensation requiring hospitalization [16], including in de novo HF [17]. Guidance for initiation and uptitration regimens was earlier informed by the TITRATION study [18].

## The preserved and mildly-reduced ejection fraction spectrum

PARAGON-HF tested ARNI in HF with preserved ejection fraction. Sacubitril–valsartan did not result in a significantly lower rate of total hospitalizations for heart failure and death from cardiovascular causes among patients with heart failure and an ejection fraction of 45% or higher [19], although signals of benefit appeared in women and in patients with lower-range ejection fraction [20]. A prespecified pooled analysis clarified the EF continuum: in more than 13,000 patients across two similarly designed trials, sacubitril/valsartan reduced HF hospitalization and cardiovascular death compared with RAAS inhibitors, with the greatest benefits observed among patients with ejection fraction below normal [21]. A sex-specific analysis examined differential effects in women versus men [22], and a participant-level pooled analysis of PARAGLIDE-HF and PARAGON-HF further explored the mildly reduced/preserved range [23]. Quality-of-life outcomes in this population showed only modest benefit [24].

## Post-myocardial infarction

PARADISE-MI examined whether ARNI benefit extends to acute MI. Patients with acute myocardial infarction complicated by reduced LVEF, pulmonary congestion, or both were randomized to sacubitril–valsartan or ramipril, and there was no significant benefit with respect to the primary outcome of cardiovascular death, first HF hospitalization, or first outpatient symptomatic heart failure [25]. An echocardiographic substudy assessed effects on cardiac structure and function after MI [26].

## Guideline recommendations and practice

Contemporary guidelines incorporate ARNI as foundational therapy. In the 2022 AHA/ACC/HFSA guideline, RAAS inhibitors that include ARNIs, ACE inhibitors, and ARBs constitute one of the four GDMT medication classes for HFrEF, alongside beta-blockers, MRAs, and SGLT2 inhibitors [27], and the document was published in parallel across journals [28]. A major change was recommending sacubitril/valsartan as first-line therapy without initial dose titration of another RAAS agent [27]. The 2021 ESC guidelines similarly endorse ARNI [29], noting that initiation in hospitalized and de novo, ACE-inhibitor-naïve patients appears safe and reduces subsequent CV death or HF hospitalizations, so initiation may be considered (class IIb) [30].

## Conclusion

Sacubitril/valsartan substantially improves outcomes in HFrEF and modulates the natriuretic peptide system to promote reverse remodeling, though its role in HFpEF and post-MI remains less certain, with benefit concentrated below normal ejection fraction. ARNI is now a cornerstone of guideline-directed therapy.
